set.text: Dana Whitfield’s new novel, The Harbor Letters, is an epistolary story: it is told entirely through letters, most of them between two sisters, one in Halifax and one in Cape Town, over thirty years. The form could have felt like a trick, but the letters have real verisimilitude. They complain about the weather, forget birthdays and repeat old jokes, just as real letters do. The book has won laudatory reviews from the literati, and it is easy to see why. Not every page succeeds. A few letters from the sisters’ father are turgid, with long, stiff sentences that slow the story down. Still, the book is full of moments worth marking. My own copy is now heavily annotated, its margins crowded with my notes and question marks. I suspect many book clubs will be passing their copies around this winter.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “verisimilitude” mean?
options: the quality of seeming real and true to life
qs.why: The letters complain, forget birthdays and repeat jokes “just as real letters do,” so they feel real. The passage is not praising beauty or length.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “turgid” mean?
options: heavy, stiff and hard to read
qs.why: The father’s letters have “long, stiff sentences that slow the story down.” That is the opposite of short and clear.

qs.q: What is the reviewer’s overall opinion of the book?
options: Mostly positive, with a few weak parts.
Perfect, with no flaws at all.
The letters feel fake and forced.
qs.why: The reviewer praises the realism and expects book clubs to share it, but says the father’s letters are weak. So the view is mostly positive, not perfect.

why: Passage said the novel is told 'entirely through letters between two sisters' but then criticizes letters from the sisters' father - self-contradiction.

set.text: For eleven years, Hana and her older brother Daniel did not speak. A fight over the sale of their parents’ house had estranged them, and the acrimony between them was so deep that relatives stopped inviting both of them to the same events. Every conversation they tried turned into recrimination: he said she had been greedy; she said he had lied. Then, last winter, Daniel’s son fell ill. Hana heard the news from a cousin and drove six hours to the hospital without a moment’s compunction about breaking her promise never to speak to him again. She sat with Daniel in the waiting room and commiserated with him, saying little, just holding his hand. Daniel later said it was her magnanimity that moved him most: she could have stayed away, and no one would have blamed her. The boy recovered. The siblings now talk every Sunday.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “recrimination” mean?
qs.why: He accused her of greed and she accused him of lying, so each answered blame with blame. It was the opposite of an apology.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “commiserated” mean?
options: shared his sadness and showed sympathy
qs.why: She sat with him and held his hand during his son’s illness, which shows sympathy. They did not argue that day.

qs.q: What ended the long silence between Hana and Daniel?
options: A court decided who owned the house.
Daniel wrote Hana a letter of apology.
Hana chose to come and support Daniel during his son’s illness.
A cousin arranged a family meeting.
Their parents asked them to make peace.
They agreed to buy the house back together.
qs.why: Hana drove to the hospital and sat with him, and Daniel was moved by her generosity. The cousin only passed on the news.

why: 'compunction' (guilt or moral hesitation about doing something wrong) was applied to simply breaking a silence, which is not a wrong; now she breaks a promise, so the card meaning fits.

set.text: When the retired engineer Farida Rahimi gave two million dollars to her hometown, local leaders were stunned by her largesse. She asked for only one thing: that the money be used where it was most needed. The town council set up a small committee to apportion the gift fairly. After months of meetings, they decided to earmark half for repairing the old public library and the rest for scholarships and a free health clinic. Each group that received money had to itemize its spending every three months, listing exactly what was bought and why. The committee would disburse the funds in stages, only after the reports arrived. Farida came to the library’s reopening and sat quietly in the back row. “She is the most beneficent person I’ve ever met,” the librarian said, “and she refuses to let us put her name on anything.”

qs.q: In the passage, what does “earmark” mean?
options: fold the corner of a page
set aside for a particular purpose
qs.why: Half the money was reserved for the library and the rest for other uses. Folding down a page corner is “dog-earing,” a different word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “itemize” mean?
options: list each item one by one
qs.why: The passage explains: “listing exactly what was bought and why.” A single total would be the opposite of a list of items.

qs.q: How did the committee make sure the money was used properly?
options: It let Farida decide every payment herself.
It paid out money in stages, only after receiving detailed spending reports.
It gave all the money to the library at once.
It put Farida’s name on every building.
It asked the librarian to check each purchase.
It spent the money before anyone could ask for it.
qs.why: Groups had to list their spending, and funds were paid only after the reports arrived. Farida asked to stay in the background.

why: earmark 'why' was muddled ('a different meaning of dog-ear, not this'); rewritten clearly.

set.text: Dr. Kwame Asante had flown overnight to give a talk at a medical conference in Geneva. He arrived bleary-eyed, his shirt rumpled from ten hours in an airplane seat. Things got worse: the speaker before him was indisposed, stuck in his hotel room with a fever, so the organizers asked Kwame to go on an hour early. He walked wearily to the stage. Then he noticed the audience. Some people were yawning; one man was openly asleep. The previous session, a long talk on billing codes, had been soporific. Kwame decided to put his slides away. He told a story instead, about a patient whose heart had stopped for six minutes and who walked out of the hospital a week later. Fidgety students in the front row sat still and leaned forward. When the talk ended, the applause woke the sleeping man, who clapped loudest of all.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “indisposed” mean?
options: slightly ill and unable to take part
qs.why: The speaker was stuck in his hotel room with a fever, so he was mildly ill and could not speak. He was not simply unwilling or late.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “soporific” mean?
options: so dull that it made people sleepy
qs.why: After that session people were yawning and one was asleep. A billing talk might have numbers, but the word means it made them sleepy.

qs.q: Why did Kwame put his slides away?
options: He saw that the audience was tired and wanted to hold their attention with a story.
His slides had been lost on the plane.
The organizers told him he had no time for slides.
He was too sleepy to read them.
He wanted to finish an hour early.
qs.why: He changed plans right after noticing yawning and a sleeping man. Nothing suggests the slides or projector had a problem.

why: 'indisposed' question: passage gave no clue to illness, so wrong options 'unwilling to speak' (a real sense of indisposed) and 'running late' also fit; passage now states he had a fever.
